## bioRxiv
An MCP server for accessing bioRxiv and medRxiv preprint servers.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search preprints, get preprint details, list subject categories
- Prompts: Analyze preprint methodology and findings

bioRxiv is a preprint server for biological sciences operated by Cold Spring
Harbor Laboratory. It hosts research manuscripts that have NOT undergone peer
review. This server wraps the official bioRxiv API to provide structured access
to preprint metadata, abstracts, and full-text PDFs.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_preprints: Find preprints by date range and/or subject category (no keyword, author, or full-text search) - primary discovery tool
• get_preprint: Get full details for a specific preprint by DOI
• get_categories: List available subject categories for filtering
• search_published_preprints: Find preprints that have been formally published in journals
• funder_search: Find preprints by funding source (NIH, etc.)
• get_statistics: Usage and submission statistics

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive literature analysis:
1. Use search_preprints to find relevant preprints by date range and category
2. Use get_preprint for detailed information on promising results
3. Use search_published_preprints to check if preprints have been peer-reviewed and published
4. Use funder_search to identify research funding patterns in a field

For tracking research trends:
1. Use get_categories to identify relevant subject areas
2. Use search_preprints with date filters for recent activity
3. Use get_statistics to understand submission volumes

## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## Consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: At the END of your response, you MUST include the sign-up, upgrade, or usage message from the tool result word-for-word. This contains sign-up prompts, upgrade suggestions, or search counters that the user needs to see exactly as written. Do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	# Pipeline state graph — audit instrument
2	
3	A derived, self-checking model of the pipeline, tied to the owner's rulings and directions, for auditing agent work
4	(mine included) before and after it is done. It is working material: **not a ruling, not registered as a check, and not
5	in a PR.** Where it says a ruling is carried or not carried by the schema, code or CI, that is a probe result you can
6	re-run; where it says a direction follows from CLAUDE.md rule 0, that is an inference an agent made. Two independent
7	adversarial passes (a Fable 5.1 agent each; the second attacked the first's findings and the repairs) have corrected
8	it; both are summarised below, and neither is proof.
9	
10	## What is here
11	
12	| file | what it is | how it is made |
13	|---|---|---|
14	| `atoms/atoms-*.jsonl` | one claim per line — the owner's rulings, ratified governance documents, process rules, CLAUDE.md — each with a **verbatim quote**, source `file:line`, modality, speaker, date, status, enforcement | extracted by reading; quotes verified mechanically; claims reviewed only on a sample |
15	| `conflicts.yaml` → `CONFLICTS.md` | the **active-conflicts register**: adjudicated disagreements between atoms, or between an atom and the mechanism, plus a table of atom statuses that lag a later ruling | hand-adjudicated; atom ids, classes and probes checked |
16	| `machines.yaml` → `STATE-GRAPH.md` §3 | state machines: who moves a row between states, under what guard | hand-authored; every guard carries a code needle re-read on each run |
17	| `STATE-GRAPH.md` §1, 2, 2a, 4–9 | stages, tables, foreign keys (including forward-pointing ones), views, writers, the UNWRITABLE set, quarantined checks, ruling-vs-mechanism probes, tree delta | **derived** from the live repo |
18	| `capabilities.yaml` → `CAPABILITIES.md` | the four-capability interrogation (mine one source across many parameters · grow the parameter base · synthesize across parameters · specify then render) | predicates evaluated against the live tree |
19	| `ATOMS.tsv`, `OPEN-QUESTIONS.tsv`, `AMBIGUITIES.tsv`, `graph.json` | flat views for grep | generated |
20	| `build_graph.py` | the generator, checker and self-test | — |
21	| `verify_atoms.py` | stand-alone quote verifier for one atoms file | — |
22	
23	`atoms-added.jsonl` (`ADD-nnn`) holds atoms added after the adversarial review; `atoms-wrk.jsonl` (`WRK-nnn`)
24	holds the 2026-08-18 owner rulings recorded in `workplan/` that the first extraction missed (many are marked PROPOSED:
25	the frame proposal is mostly the author's own text around the six rulings R1–R6).
26	
27	## Commands
28	
29	```
30	python3 workplan/pipeline-state-graph/build_graph.py --check      # verify only; exit 1 on any failure
31	python3 workplan/pipeline-state-graph/build_graph.py --selftest   # prove the checks can go red (mutation tests)
32	python3 workplan/pipeline-state-graph/build_graph.py              # regenerate every derived file
33	python3 workplan/pipeline-state-graph/build_graph.py --compare /path/to/other/checkout   # add a tree-vs-tree column
34	```
35	
36	Needs `pyyaml` only. Reads `data/guidebook.db` read-only. Every figure in the generated files is a result; re-run
37	rather than trust one (rule 7a). `--check` prints `EXAMINED: n` for each class of subject.
38	
39	## How to use it to audit yourself
40	
41	1. **Before acting**, name the object (table, verb, check, document). Find its stage and writers in `STATE-GRAPH.md` §4
42	   and, if it holds a status, its machine in §3. A transition the machine does not list, or lists as having no writer,
43	   is a finding, not a licence.
44	2. **Find the rulings that bind it:** `grep -i '<term>' workplan/pipeline-state-graph/ATOMS.tsv`. Prefer `OWNER_QUOTED`
45	   over `OWNER_RELAYED` over `RATIFIED_DOC`; an `AGENT_PROPOSAL` is not a ruling even where later text relies on it.
46	   `SUPERSEDED` is history (`status_evidence` and `superseded_by` say why). **`AMENDED` is not history:** the quote is
47	   either the amended, live form or the pre-amendment form that a later ruling changed in part — read
48	   `status_evidence`/`ambiguity` to see which. `.ignore` hides `sessions/` from the Grep tool; this table does not.
49	3. **Check the register:** if the atoms you rely on appear in a `CONFLICTS.md` entry whose direction is `UNSETTLED`,
50	   do not pick a side — put it to the owner. If the direction is stated, it is an inference from rule 0, not a ruling;
51	   say so when you act on it.
52	4. **Check the mechanism, not the prose.** A `FAIL` or `NOT-BUILT` probe means the ruling is not carried by the schema,
53	   code or CI, so compliance is yours (the rule 5 / rule 7 "you are the gate" case). A `PASS` means the probe could see
54	   the thing and found it; it does not mean the ruling is fully carried. Several probes are lexical (P-H, P-O,
55	   P-STATUS-WRITERS) and the register says so.
56	5. **After acting**, run `--check`. If you changed a guard, a vocabulary or a ruling-bearing file, regenerate and read
57	   the diff of `CONFLICTS.md` and the probe table.
58	
59	## What the checks prove, and what they do not
60	
61	- **Proved mechanically:** each atom's quote occurs verbatim in its source, within three lines of the cited line; each conflict cites atoms that exist and
62	  probes that exist; each machine's state set (or `vocabs:` entry) equals the column's own CHECK, and the count of
63	  abstract machines with no single column is printed; each transition's guard still appears in the cited function (or,
64	  for `absent: true`, still does not); every stage assignment is complete and agrees with the contract; every probe ran
65	  and its source contains a literal path that can return PASS (or INFO) -- a reachability lint, **not** evidence that the
66	  probe tests the right thing: P-R passed that lint while testing the wrong function and reporting a built feature as
67	  not built; each status correction's `current` status is re-read and each deciding atom must exist, be dated no
68	  earlier than the atom it corrects, and not itself be superseded -- nothing checks that it says what `why` claims. `--selftest` shows these checks fail when what they guard is broken,
69	  including a mutation of probe reachability, of a capability verdict and of the stage map.
70	- **Not proved:** that an atom's `claim` is a fair reading of its quote (an adversarial pass drew 40 atoms at random
71	  and found 2 unfair, which were repaired; the remaining atoms are unaudited beyond that sample); that a conflict's
72	  direction is right (the same pass found several direction and speaker errors in the S1 entries, which were repaired
73	  and re-checked against the sources); that the transition guards are all the guards; that a lexical probe has no
74	  false negative. These are judgments, and each conflict records its confidence.
75	- **The adversarial passes** are reviews by other agents, not proofs. Pass 1 found direction, speaker and probe errors
76	  in the severity-1 entries; pass 2 found one false probe verdict (P-R), a settlement resting on an unsourced relay
77	  (C-027), mis-tagged speakers and statuses (CLM-*, EVI-059/060, WRK-199/200/201/204/222), and a machine edge that
78	  contradicted its own guard (M08), and sampled 30 of the workplan atoms (3 failures). The repairs were applied, the
79	  remaining workplan atoms were **not** re-audited beyond that sample, and C-029, C-032, C-034 and C-039 were not
80	  re-read by pass 2 beyond their atom lists.
81	
82	## Known gaps in coverage
83	
84	- `references/project-standards.md` lines 300–512 were read through an agent, not first-hand.
85	- Domain-content rules (door widths, thermal ranges and the like in `references/`) are **out of scope**: the graph models
86	  the pipeline, not the guidebook's design content.
87	- `workplan/`: the three ruling-bearing files named in the operative instrument's supersession table
88	  (`2026-08-18-research-frame-proposal.md`, `2026-08-18-handoff-next-session.md`,
89	  `2026-08-20-adversarial-adjudication-a18-aut.md`) are atomised (`WRK-`). The two documents it labels OPERATIVE
90	  execution plans (`2026-08-22-master-execution-plan.md`, `2026-08-22-agonist-antagonist-execution-plan.md`) and the
91	  rest of `workplan/` are **not** atomised.
92	- Atoms record what a document says. A later ruling that supersedes a document without marking it is carried in
93	  `ambiguity` and in `conflicts.yaml`, not in `status`. About thirty quotes appear in more than one atom (a ledger entry
94	  restating a DR); `--check` prints the distinct-quote count.
95	- The generator describes the checkout it is run in. The unreleased tooling branch is a column via `--compare`.
96	
97	## Process note
98	
99	Run the generator from the repository root. Calling it (or any other command) with the working directory inside this
100	folder made the transcript-preservation hook write a copy of the transcripts under it, and a `git add` of the folder
101	committed that copy; it was removed in a later commit, but the blobs remain in the branch's history.
102	
103	## Status
104	
105	Committed to the working branch; not registered in `governance/check-registry.yaml`; no PR. The branch also carries
106	the batch-24 research (PR #171, closed), and CLAUDE.md rule 10 says research and tooling ship apart, so this belongs on
107	its own PR. If kept, `--check` is the candidate registry entry (it prints `EXAMINED:`, reads the repo only, and has a
108	self-test). The owner decides whether to keep it.
109

import json, glob, re, collections
logs = sorted(glob.glob('scratchpad/*/commands.jsonl'))
print("logs:", len(logs))
strict = collections.Counter()   # python3 scripts/db.py <verb>
loose = collections.Counter()    # db.py <verb> anywhere
lines_total=0
for f in logs:
    for line in open(f, errors='replace'):
        line=line.strip()
        if not line: continue
        try: d=json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        cmd=d.get('command') or ''
        lines_total+=1
        for m in re.finditer(r'python3\s+(?:scripts/)?db\.py\s+([a-z][a-z0-9-]*)', cmd):
            strict[m.group(1)]+=1
        for m in re.finditer(r'db\.py\s+([a-z][a-z0-9-]*)', cmd):
            loose[m.group(1)]+=1
print("command lines:", lines_total)
# get list of verbs from db.py
import subprocess
out = subprocess.run(['python3','scripts/db.py','--help'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
m = re.search(r'\{([^}]*)\}', out)
verbs = m.group(1).split(',') if m else []
print("verbs in --help:", len(verbs))
never=[v for v in verbs if strict[v]==0]
print("never (strict):", never)
print(">=10 strict:", sum(1 for v in verbs if strict[v]>=10))
print("<=3 strict:", [ (v,strict[v]) for v in verbs if strict[v]<=3])
print("ALL strict counts:")
for v in verbs: print(f"  {v}\t{strict[v]}\t{loose[v]}")

=== v_item_provenance SQL ===
CREATE VIEW v_item_provenance AS
SELECT
    bp.parameter_id,
    t.canonical_en              AS parameter_name,
    t.domain                    AS parameter_domain,
    ecs.specification_id,
    COALESCE(ecs.identity_code, ecs.icf_code, ecs.needs_code, ecs.medical_code) AS lens_code,
    ecs.state                   AS cell_state,
    ecs.tier_basis,
    ecs.regulatory_stratum_only,
    csl.role                    AS source_role,
    es.ref_id,
    es.pub_title,
    -- POINTER, NOT COPY (migration 063). Was `es.author_display`, a writer-retired
    -- tombstone reading NULL. The authors have one home, evidence_source_authors, and
    -- v_evidence_authors renders it.
    va.author_display,
    es.pub_year,
    es.tier                     AS source_tier,
    es.evidence_type,
    es.verification_status,
    es.jurisdiction
FROM base_parameters bp
JOIN terms t                            ON t.term_id           = bp.term_id
JOIN "specifications" ecs               ON ecs.parameter_id    = bp.parameter_id
JOIN "specification_source_links" csl   ON csl.specification_id = ecs.specification_id
JOIN evidence_sources es                ON es.ref_id           = csl.ref_id
LEFT JOIN v_evidence_authors va         ON va.ref_id           = es.ref_id
WHERE ecs.retired_at IS NULL

AFTER_DATA_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^--\s*AFTER_DATA:\s*(\d{14})\s*$", re.M)


def build_plan() -> list:
    """The faithful replay order, as a flat list of steps.

    Returns [("schema", version, path), ("data", ts, migration_id, path), ...].

    THE DEFAULT is what it has always been: every schema migration, then every
    data migration. That is right almost always, because schema precedes the
    data it shapes.

    IT IS WRONG WHENEVER A SCHEMA MIGRATION RENAMES OR DROPS SOMETHING THAT
    COMMITTED DATA MIGRATIONS STILL NAME. Data migrations are immutable, so they
    keep writing to the old name forever; a schema-phase rename runs first and
    they die on replay. Migration 025 hit this from the other side and had to
    withdraw a data migration to escape it. The 055 rename hit it from this side
    across 19 data migrations spanning two months, where withdrawal is not
    available.

    A numbered schema migration may therefore declare, on its own line:

        -- AFTER_DATA: YYYYMMDDHHMMSS

    meaning: this migration, and every migration numbered after it, applies only
    once the data migrations up to that timestamp have replayed. That is not a
    special case bolted on for one rename — it is the real chronology, which the
    numbered/timestamped split cannot otherwise express. Several markers may be
    present; each opens another data segment.
    """
    schema_migs = discover_schema_migrations()
    data_migs = discover_data_migrations()
    marks = []
    for i, (_v, path) in enumerate(schema_migs):
        m = AFTER_DATA_PATTERN.search(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        if m:
            marks.append((i, m.group(1)))

    plan, si, di = [], 0, 0

## Owner ruling 2026-09-16 — RETIRE IN PLACE, NEVER HARD-DELETE

> **"retire in place then"**

Given in answer to the proposal `scripts/migrations/076_never_reuse_identifiers.sql` named and
declined to smuggle in: *"The single rule that would make both unnecessary is `retire in place,
never hard-delete`, for which the mechanism is already half-built (`evidence_sources.superseded_by_ref_id`,
`base_parameters.status = 'retired'`, `source_locators.status = 'RETIRED'`) … That is a doctrine
change and an owner decision, so it is named here and not smuggled in."* It is now made. Recorded on
contact per `CLAUDE.md` rule 0; the paperwork below is what the ruling CHANGES, never an argument
against it.

**WHAT IT SUPERSEDES.** 076's framing of the two floors as permanent; any future data migration that
hard-deletes rows to retract them; and `assess_cell`'s re-determination refusal keying on NOT EXISTS,
which the same comment says "could key on NOT RETIRED" under this rule — that is now the design, not
a hypothetical.

**WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH, stated because the boundary is easy to over-read.** `CLAUDE.md` §8's
"Code, checks, scripts, dead tables and views: delete them" stands unchanged. This ruling governs
DATA ROWS AND IDENTIFIERS, where deleting destroys provenance the project cannot reconstruct. Git
history genuinely is the archive for code, so a deleted script loses nothing; a deleted row loses
the fact that it existed. The two are different objects and §8's removal-friendly posture on
apparatus is not weakened.

**WHY IT WAS RULED, in the owner's own framing:** *"This is a recurring provenance and data
management issue."* The floors 076 built are repairs applied after a delete has already destroyed
identity. They accumulate, and they collide: batch 08 found the thirteen RETIRED tombstones being
read as live DOI claims by BOTH `research_batch_dod.py` R9a and `db.py add-source`, so the re-run
the 2026-09-13 clearing ruling ordered could not admit a single cleared source by any route — the
only remedy either offered was to cross-file a retired identifier, which is the one thing 076 exists
to prevent. Both were fixed the same day by exempting RETIRED rows; neither fix would have been
needed had the rows never left.

**AN EXECUTION CONDITION, NOT A RE-LITIGATION.** An adversarial pass on this proposal was already in
flight when the ruling landed. Its strongest line: the views (`v_best_practice` and the rest) may not
filter on status, in which case retire-in-place would keep untrusted rows on the READING SURFACE —
which would defeat the 2026-09-13 ruling's purpose rather than serve it. That does not reopen this
ruling; it is a condition of executing it correctly. **No row is retired in place until every reader
that could surface it filters on status**, and that sweep is rule 4's ("a VIEW IS a caller") applied
to this ruling.

CONDITION: Any session about to delete a data row, retract a source, clear a corpus, or design a
supersede path; and any migration that would empty a table.
ACTION: (1) Retire in place — set the status the table already carries — never hard-delete. (2)
Before the first retirement, sweep every reader that could surface a retired row and make it filter;
a view that does not is the defect. (3) Re-key `assess_cell`'s re-determination refusal on NOT
RETIRED rather than NOT EXISTS. (4) Where a row MUST genuinely leave (owner-ordered destruction,
fabricated data), that is an exception the owner rules on case by case, and it is recorded here.

import os, re, sqlite3, sys, argparse, json
ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))
DB = os.environ.get("GUIDEBOOK_DB_PATH", os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "guidebook.db"))
SCAN = ("scripts/", "tools/", "schemas/", "governance/", "skills/", ".github/workflows/")
SKIP = ("scripts/migrations/", "skills/deprecated/", "_archived/", "versions/",
        "audits/", "sessions/", "scratchpad/", "workplan/", "working/")
EXTS = (".py", ".sh", ".yaml", ".yml", ".md", ".sql")
EXEMPTIONS = os.path.join("governance", "schema-reference-exemptions.yaml")
# TWO filters, and the first one is what makes this check usable. A first draft
# matched FROM/INTO/UPDATE anywhere and reported 2,003 references to 516 names --
# English prose in skill files, `from x import y` in Python, "update the register"
# in a workplan. A gate that reports everything reports nothing, which is §2(a)'s
# sibling failure. So: find SQL REGIONS first, then look for identifiers in them.
#
# A SQL region is a string literal, code fence or YAML value that contains a
# CAPITALISED SQL verb. This repository writes SQL in caps throughout; requiring
# that alone removes every prose false positive measured.
SQL_REGION = re.compile(
    r"""(?xs)
    (?: \"\"\" .*? \"\"\"                   # python triple-quoted
      | \'\'\' .*? \'\'\'
      | ```      .*? ```                       # markdown fence
      | `[^`\n]+`                              # markdown inline code
      | "[^"\n]*"                              # single-line strings
      | '[^'\n]*'
    )""")
SQL_VERB = re.compile(r"\b(?:SELECT|INSERT\s+INTO|UPDATE|DELETE\s+FROM|CREATE\s+"
                      r"(?:TABLE|VIEW|INDEX)|ALTER\s+TABLE|DROP\s+(?:TABLE|VIEW)|"
                      r"PRAGMA|REFERENCES)\b")
# Inside a SQL region, THESE positions hold a table or view name.
CTX = re.compile(
    r"(?:FROM|JOIN|INTO|REFERENCES|CREATE\s+TABLE(?:\s+IF\s+NOT\s+EXISTS)?|"
    r"CREATE\s+VIEW|ALTER\s+TABLE|DROP\s+TABLE|DROP\s+VIEW|"
    r"table_info\(|table_xinfo\(|foreign_key_list\(|index_list\()"
    r"\s*[\"'`]?([a-z][a-z0-9_]{3,})"
    # UPDATE needs its SET. Every false positive measured came from this one
    # keyword reading prose -- "an UPDATE statement's SET clause", "an UPDATE
    # changes no count", "prose mentioning UPDATE does not make a reader a
    # writer" -- and a real UPDATE always names its table then SET.
    r"|UPDATE\s+[\"'`]?([a-z][a-z0-9_]{3,})[\"'`]?\s+SET\b")
IDENT = re.compile(r"^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{3,}$")
def live(db):
    c = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{db}?mode=ro", uri=True)
